templates.title: Prompt caching that costs more than it saves
templates.subtopic: conditional cost arithmetic, grouping through a lookup, numeric rounding

sections.scenario: API customers can mark the stable start of a prompt (a long system prompt, a contract, a codebase) for caching. Public documentation describes the billing shape: writing a prefix to the cache costs more than ordinary input tokens, and reading it back costs much less, with a longer cache duration priced higher than the default one. Each response reports its usage split into ordinary input tokens, cache-write tokens, cache-read tokens and output tokens. A platform team keeps a warehouse copy of that usage and wants to know, per workspace and model, whether caching is saving money or quietly costing more: a prefix that is written again and again but never read back is pure overhead.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query over the UTC day {{day}} that returns one row per (workspace_id, model) with at least {{min_requests}} requests that day: workspace_id (the API key's workspace), model, requests, prompt_tokens (input + 5-minute writes + 1-hour writes + cache reads), cache_read_share = ROUND(cache reads / prompt_tokens, 4), actual_cost_usd, uncached_cost_usd and net_savings_usd = uncached − actual. Prices are in US dollars per million tokens. In this exercise a 5-minute cache write costs 1.25 × the model's input price, a 1-hour cache write 2 ×, a cache read 0.1 ×; output tokens cost the output price. The uncached cost bills every prompt token at the input price, plus the same output cost. Round the three money columns to 4 decimal places, computing net_savings_usd from the unrounded costs. Order by net_savings_usd, then workspace_id, then model. {{write_rule}} {{workspace_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Do every calculation in numeric; never in floating point and never with integer division. The day is half-open: [{{day}} 00:00, next day 00:00) UTC. The sample has {{n_requests}} usage rows; production has hundreds of millions per day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical prices, models, workspaces and usage. The multipliers are this exercise's and follow the shape described in public pricing pages; real prices change, so check current documentation. The warehouse table stores the usage block of each response in its own columns, one row per request. Output tokens are the same with or without caching, so they cancel out of the savings.
sections.criteria: Attributes requests through the key's workspace; aggregates before pricing; correct per-class multipliers including the longer duration; uncached cost bills all prompt tokens at the input price; numeric arithmetic with the stated rounding; half-open day; inclusive minimum; deterministic ordering with negative savings first; explains what the result means for a customer.

clarifications.q: Which workspace does a request belong to?
clarifications.a: The workspace of the API key that sent it, from api_keys. A workspace can have several keys.

clarifications.q: Is a cache read free?
clarifications.a: No. In this exercise it costs 0.1 × the input price; it is cheap, not free.

clarifications.q: What is the "uncached" cost of a cache read token?
clarifications.a: The full input price: without caching, that token would have been sent as ordinary input.

clarifications.q: Is the minimum inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A group with exactly {{min_requests}} requests is reported.

clarifications.q: Can net savings be negative?
clarifications.a: Yes, and those rows are the point of the report: they sort first.

hints: Aggregate tokens per (workspace, model) first, then join the price once per group; prices are per model, so the cost is a linear function of the sums.
The uncached cost is (input + writes + reads) × input price + output × output price; the actual cost weights each class by its multiplier.
Cast before dividing for the share: reads::numeric / prompt_tokens.
followups: Finance asks for the same report monthly per workspace across all models. What changes, and which columns can you no longer add up from the daily rows?
A workspace shows a large negative saving. List three causes you could tell apart from this table alone, and the query that tells them apart.
The longer cache duration costs more to write. Using this data, how would you estimate, per workspace, whether it would pay for itself?
Usage arrives late and is occasionally restated. How would you build this as an incremental daily table that stays correct?

rules.ask: A workspace has two keys, and some keys belong to no named workspace. Which rows does your join and grouping produce for them?
Why does floating point matter for a money column rounded to 4 places, and where in your query could it change a result?
Which rows at exactly midnight does your day filter include, and on which day do they belong?
Cache pricing differs by duration and changes over time. Where would you keep these multipliers so a price change does not mean rewriting the query?

templates.title: Streams that stalled after the first token
templates.subtopic: LAG over a filtered event stream, per-request outcomes, NULL-aware filters

sections.scenario: When a client asks for a streamed response, the API sends server-sent events: message_start, then for each content block a content_block_start, a series of content_block_delta events carrying the text, and a content_block_stop, then message_delta and message_stop. Public documentation also describes ping events, which can arrive at any time and carry no content, and error events. A streaming-observability team logs every event a sampled client receives and wants two numbers per stream: the time to the first token, and the longest silence between two pieces of text, because a stream that starts quickly and then stalls for seconds feels broken to users.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns one row for every request that is a problem: request_id, model, ttft_ms (milliseconds from started_at to the first content_block_delta; NULL if there is none), max_gap_ms (the largest gap in milliseconds between two consecutive content_block_delta events of the request, in seq order; NULL with fewer than two), deltas (the number of content_block_delta events) and outcome: 'completed' if the stream has a message_stop, otherwise 'error' if it has an error event, otherwise 'truncated'. A request is a problem if its outcome is not 'completed', or ttft_ms > {{ttft_ms}}, or max_gap_ms > {{gap_ms}}. Return both durations as whole milliseconds (bigint). Order by request_id. {{edge_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). seq orders the events of one request; event_ts never decreases along seq. Thresholds are strict. The sample has {{n_requests}} requests and {{n_events}} events; production samples millions of streams a day.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical models, timings and thresholds. Event names follow the public streaming documentation; the table is a client-side log of what was received, one row per event. Every request is complete in the log: nothing more will arrive.
sections.criteria: TTFT from started_at to the first delta; gaps from LAG over deltas only, in seq order; NULL-aware handling of streams with zero or one delta; correct three-way outcome; requests without events kept; strict thresholds; integer milliseconds; deterministic ordering; can explain why pings must not count as progress.

clarifications.q: Does a ping count as progress?
clarifications.a: No. A ping carries no content; a stall with pings in it is still a stall. Only content_block_delta events count.

clarifications.q: When does the TTFT clock start?
clarifications.a: At started_at, when the client sent the request, not at message_start.

clarifications.q: Two events have the same event_ts. Which is first?
clarifications.a: The one with the lower seq. Their gap is 0.

clarifications.q: A stream has one delta and then completes. Is its gap 0?
clarifications.a: No, it has no gap: max_gap_ms is NULL, and NULL is not over the threshold.

clarifications.q: A request never received any event. Is it in the result?
clarifications.a: Yes: it has no message_stop and no error, so it is 'truncated'.

hints: Filter to content_block_delta first, then LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY request_id ORDER BY seq). LAG over all events lets a ping split a silence.
EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM interval) * 1000 gives milliseconds; cast to bigint.
Start from stream_requests and LEFT JOIN the per-request aggregates, so requests without deltas or without events survive.
followups: The same report every minute over a live stream of events. What state do you keep per open request, and when can you emit a row?
Product wants a p50 and p99 TTFT per model per hour on a dashboard. Why can you not average hourly percentiles into a daily one, and what would you store instead?
A long stall appears only for very long outputs. How would you separate model generation time from network or client problems using only this log?
The log is sampled at 1% of streams. Which of your metrics stay unbiased, and which need care?

rules.ask: Did you filter to deltas before or after the window function? Walk me through a 9-second silence with pings every second.
Why measure from started_at rather than message_start, and what would the difference hide?
A request that never received a single event: where is it in your result?
Two deltas share a millisecond. Is your LAG order deterministic, and does it matter for the gap?

templates.title: Message batch reconciliation across resubmissions
templates.subtopic: latest attempt per item, anti-joins for missing results, first-of-many with tie-breaks

sections.scenario: The Message Batches API processes many requests asynchronously. Each request in a batch carries a custom_id, unique within that batch, and once the batch has ended each request has one result whose type is succeeded, errored, canceled or expired (public documentation says requests not processed within 24 hours expire). A customer's nightly job submits its items as one batch, then resubmits the items that did not succeed in later batches. Their data team needs to know, per job, where every item stands, and whether a client bug is paying for the same item twice.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns one row per job_id: items (distinct custom_ids submitted by the job's batches), and a classification of each item into exactly one of succeeded (it has a succeeded result in any of the job's batches), retry (no success; its latest attempt has a result), missing (no success; its latest attempt is in an ended batch but has no result row) or in_flight (no success; its latest attempt is in a batch that has not ended). Also duplicate_successes (items with more than one succeeded result) and wasted_output_tokens (the output tokens of every success after an item's first). An item's attempts are ordered by the batch's created_at, then batch_id. Order by job_id. {{status_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). An item is identified by (job_id, custom_id). items = succeeded + retry + missing + in_flight for every job. The sample has {{n_batches}} batches and {{n_requests}} batch requests.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical jobs, ids and token counts. Batch statuses and result types follow the public documentation, simplified to in_progress and ended. Results exist only for ended batches. In this exercise every success is billed, so a second success for the same item is wasted spend.
sections.criteria: One row per attempt with a LEFT JOIN to results; latest attempt with a full tie-break; succeeded wins over a later failure; missing and in-flight separated by batch status; distinct items per job; first success by the same ordering; categories that add up to items; deterministic ordering; can discuss idempotent resubmission.

clarifications.q: An item succeeded, was resubmitted by mistake, and the resubmission errored. What is it?
clarifications.a: Succeeded. Once an item has a success, it has its answer.

clarifications.q: Two batches of the same job were created in the same second. Which is later?
clarifications.a: The one with the greater batch_id. The result must be deterministic.

clarifications.q: Is an item whose latest batch is still in progress missing?
clarifications.a: No. Results do not exist until a batch has ended, so it is in flight.

clarifications.q: Which success is "first" for wasted tokens?
clarifications.a: The earliest by created_at, then batch_id. Every later success is wasted.

hints: Build one row per attempt: batch_requests joined to batches, LEFT JOIN batch_results. An inner join to results loses exactly the items you are asked to find.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY job_id, custom_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, batch_id DESC) = 1 is the latest attempt; the same window ascending over successes numbers them.
Reduce to one row per item, then count with FILTER per job.
followups: Jobs submit millions of items a night. How would you make this report incremental, touching only batches that ended since the last run?
How should the client choose what to resubmit, so that a duplicate success cannot happen? What does the batch result give you to make the resubmission idempotent?
A batch has ended, and 0.1% of its requests have no result in your warehouse. How do you tell an export problem from an API problem, and what alert would you add?
Expired results cluster at certain hours. What would you look at before deciding to split jobs into smaller batches?

rules.ask: An item in an ended batch with no result row: where does it appear in your result?
An item succeeded in its first batch and failed in its second. What does "latest attempt" say about it, and what should the report say?
An item submitted in three batches: how many items does your count give for it?
Two batches of one job share a created_at. Which success is first in your query, and is that the same on every run?

templates.title: Tool-use calls: outcomes per tool and peak calls in flight
templates.subtopic: matching events by id, interval overlap

sections.scenario: With tool use, the model replies with a tool_use block that has an id, a tool name and an input; the application runs the tool and sends back a tool_result block that refers to that id, optionally marked is_error. An agent platform logs both sides of every call and wants a dashboard per tool (how many calls succeeded, errored or timed out) and one capacity number: the most tool calls that were ever in flight at the same moment, which sizes the pool of workers that execute them.
sections.problem: Implement tool_call_stats(events, timeout_ms). events is a list of (ts_ms, conversation_id, kind, tool_use_id, tool_name, is_error) sorted by ts_ms (ties in list order), with kind 'use' or 'result'. A use starts a call. A result finishes the call it refers to: if it arrives at most timeout_ms after the use, the call is ok (or an error if is_error); if it arrives later, the call counts as timed out and the result is ignored. A call that never gets a result timed out. A call is in flight over the half-open interval [use_ts, end), where end is its result's time if it finished in time and use_ts + timeout_ms if it timed out. Return (per_tool, unmatched_results, peak_in_flight): per_tool[tool_name] = [calls, ok, errors, timed_out] for every tool with at least one call, the number of results that refer to no earlier use, and the largest number of calls in flight at any instant (0 if none). Only a call's first result counts; a later one for the same call is ignored. {{dup_rule}} {{key_rule}} In the tests, timeout_ms = {{timeout_ms}}.
sections.constraints: Up to about 220 000 events and hundreds of calls in flight at once. Expected: O(n log n) time and O(n) memory.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical tools, timeouts and traffic. The log is complete: every result that will ever arrive is in it.
sections.criteria: Correct matching with duplicate uses and results ignored; inclusive timeout boundary; late results become timeouts and are not unmatched; unmatched counted only for results with no earlier use; half-open intervals with ends before starts at equal times; O(n log n) with a justification; discusses streaming and bounded state.

clarifications.q: Is a result exactly timeout_ms after the use on time?
clarifications.a: Yes. Only strictly later is a timeout.

clarifications.q: Does a late result count as unmatched?
clarifications.a: No. It matches its call, which is already timed out; the result is ignored.

clarifications.q: A call ends at the same millisecond another starts. Do they overlap?
clarifications.a: No. Intervals are half-open, so the first is no longer in flight.

clarifications.q: A result and its use have the same timestamp. Is the call ever in flight?
clarifications.a: No. Its interval is empty.

clarifications.q: The same use appears twice. Two calls?
clarifications.a: No. A use whose call already exists is ignored.

hints: A dict keyed by (conversation_id, tool_use_id) matches results to uses in O(1).
Once every call's interval is known, turn each into a +1 at its start and a −1 at its end, sort, and sweep. At equal times the −1 must come first.
Calls that never get a result also need intervals: [use_ts, use_ts + timeout_ms).
followups: Compute the peak on a live stream instead, without waiting for the log to be complete. What do you keep in memory, and when is a call's end known?
The worker pool is shared by 40 tools with different latencies. How would you report the peak per tool and the peak overall in one pass?
Telemetry from two collectors disagrees by up to 200 ms. Which of your numbers change, and how would you make them robust?
Results for unknown ids keep growing. What could cause them, and how would you find out which?

rules.ask: How many events does your matching look at per result when 500 calls are in flight?
Two events at the same millisecond, one ending a call and one starting another. Which comes first in your sort, and why?
When you push a call into the heap, do you already know when it ends? What do you do about results that arrive after the timeout?
What does your dict hold after a call finishes, and how large does it grow in a week of traffic?

templates.title: Prompt-cache replay: reads, writes and uncached input
templates.subtopic: longest live prefix with expiry, linear work per prompt

sections.scenario: Prompt caching stores a prompt's prefix so a later request that starts with exactly the same content can read it instead of processing it again. Public documentation describes the behaviour this exercise simplifies: a cached prefix lives for a few minutes by default (a longer duration is available), using it refreshes its lifetime, prefixes below a minimum length are not cached, and a request that misses writes the prefix. Before a customer turns caching on for a long-running chat assistant, an analyst wants to replay last week's prompts through a model of the cache and see how many tokens would have been read, written and sent as ordinary input.
sections.problem: Implement cache_accounting(requests, min_tokens=0). Each request is (ts_s, workspace_id, segments, ttl_s) with segments a non-empty list of (segment_id, tokens); requests are sorted by ts_s and processed in list order. The prompt is the concatenation of its segments. Prefix k is segments 0..k; only prefixes ending before the last segment can be cached (the last segment is the new turn and is always ordinary input). A prefix is cacheable if its cumulative tokens are at least min_tokens. A cache entry is identified by the workspace and the exact sequence of segment ids, and is live while ts < expires_at. For each request: the hit is its longest cacheable prefix with a live entry; cache_read is the hit prefix's tokens (0 if none); cache_write is the tokens of its longest cacheable prefix minus cache_read (0 if there is nothing beyond the hit); everything else is uncached_input. Then every cacheable prefix of the request is stored or refreshed with expires_at = ts + ttl_s. Return one (cache_read, cache_write, uncached_input) per request. {{min_rule}} {{ws_rule}} {{ttl_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to a few thousand requests whose prompts have up to about 1 200 segments each (long conversations); about two million segments in total. Expected: work proportional to the number of segments in each prompt, not to its square.
sections.assumptions: A deliberately simplified, hypothetical cache model: every segment boundary acts as a breakpoint (the real API limits how many you can mark), there is no eviction other than expiry, and the cache is scoped to a workspace. TTLs, the minimum and the traffic are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Correct longest live cacheable prefix; strict expiry; reads and writes as defined, with the last segment never cached; refresh of every cacheable prefix; workspace isolation; cumulative minimum; at the Very Hard level, expiry never shortened; linear work per prompt with a clear argument; honest discussion of what the simplified model over- or under-states.

clarifications.q: Does a hit refresh the entry?
clarifications.a: Yes. Every cacheable prefix of the request, hit or written, is refreshed to ts + ttl_s (the TTL rule above says what happens when requests use different TTLs).

clarifications.q: Is an entry live at exactly expires_at?
clarifications.a: No. It is live while ts < expires_at; at exactly 300 seconds after a 300-second write it has expired.

clarifications.q: Is the minimum about one segment or the whole prefix?
clarifications.a: The whole prefix: its cumulative tokens from segment 0.

clarifications.q: Two requests in different workspaces send the same segments. Do they share an entry?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise: entries are per workspace.

clarifications.q: A request repeats the previous prompt exactly. What is read?
clarifications.a: Everything except the last segment, which is never cached.

hints: Build the key for prefix k from the key for prefix k − 1 in O(1): a trie of segment ids per workspace, where each node stores its expiry, or an integer id per (parent id, segment id) pair.
Walk the prompt once from the start: track the cumulative tokens, the deepest cacheable node with a live entry, and the deepest cacheable node; then refresh the cacheable nodes you passed.
tuple(ids[:k + 1]) as a key costs O(k) to build and to hash, for every k: that is quadratic per prompt.
followups: The replay says caching would save 70% of input tokens. Which simplifications in this model make that number optimistic?
The real API lets you mark only a few breakpoints. Given this trace, how would you choose where to put them for one conversation?
Memory: the trie keeps every prefix ever seen. How would you prune it without changing any answer?
Price the replay with the longer cache duration on some requests. How would you decide, per conversation, which duration pays for itself?

rules.ask: What does building and hashing that key cost for a prompt with 1 000 segments, and how many times do you do it per request?
Your trie never deletes nodes. How large is it after a week, and what could you remove safely?
What happens if two different prefixes collide, and how would you detect or bound that?
A 1-hour entry is hit by a request with a 5-minute TTL. What must happen to its expiry, and why?

templates.title: Deadline-first scheduling of batch jobs under per-model concurrency
templates.subtopic: earliest deadline first, per-model slots, cancellation

sections.scenario: A platform team runs a job runner in front of a model API for the rest of the company. Teams submit jobs (a list of model requests to process, each job with a deadline its owner chose); the runner sends the requests one by one, and to stay inside the organization's rate limits it allows only a fixed number of requests in flight per model. When the backlog is long, the order matters: the runner serves the waiting job with the earliest deadline first, and requests that have not started by their job's deadline are dropped and reported as expired, much as public asynchronous batch interfaces report requests that were not processed in time. Before changing the slot limits, the team wants an exact replay of a day of submissions that says, per job, how many requests ran, were canceled or expired, and when the last one finished. {{model_rule}}
sections.problem:
Implement run_jobs(jobs, slots, cancels). Each job is (job_id, model, submit_ts, deadline_ts, durations): durations lists the run time of each of its requests, in seconds, in the order they must start. slots[model] is how many requests of that model may run at once. Time is in whole seconds. At every second t at which something happens, in this order:

  1. Requests that finish at t free their slots.
  2. Jobs submitted at t join their model's queue.
  3. Cancels at t apply: if t < deadline_ts, every request of that job that has not started becomes canceled; a cancel at or after the deadline changes nothing.
  4. Each model fills its free slots, one request at a time, from the waiting job with the earliest deadline_ts; ties go to the earlier submit_ts, then to the job listed first in jobs. A request may start only if t < deadline_ts; once a job's deadline has passed, all its requests that have not started are expired. A started request always runs to completion, even past the deadline.

Return {job_id: (done, canceled, expired, last_finish)} for every job, where last_finish is the latest finish time of its done requests, or None if none ran. {{cancel_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 8 000 jobs and 200 000 requests; thousands of jobs can be waiting at once. Durations are positive integers; slots has a positive entry for every model used. Expected: O(R log J) for R requests and J jobs. Scanning the waiting jobs at every start is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Jobs, models, durations, deadlines and slot counts are hypothetical. The runner is the team's own scheduler, not a description of how any provider processes batches; it simply honours per-model concurrency as a way of staying under rate limits. A job's requests start in list order, and only one cancel per job exists.
sections.criteria: Event-driven simulation that jumps between submissions, finishes and cancels; finishes before submissions before cancels before starts within one second; a finish-time heap per model and a deadline-ordered heap of waiting jobs with the full tie-break; strict t < deadline_ts for starting, started requests always complete; cancels only before the deadline and only for requests not yet started; models independent; correct None for jobs with nothing done; O(R log J); can explain where earliest-deadline-first is and is not optimal.

clarifications.q: A request finishes at second 10. Can the next one start at 10?
clarifications.a: Yes. Finished requests free their slots first, then slots are filled.

clarifications.q: Can a request start exactly at the deadline?
clarifications.a: No. It must start strictly before deadline_ts. One that started at deadline_ts − 1 runs to completion.

clarifications.q: A cancel and a possible start happen at the same second. Which wins?
clarifications.a: The cancel. Cancels apply before slots are filled.

clarifications.q: What does a cancel do to requests that are already running?
clarifications.a: Nothing. They finish and count as done.

clarifications.q: Can a model with free slots help another model?
clarifications.a: No. Each model has its own slots.

clarifications.q: Do I need to simulate every second?
clarifications.a: No. Nothing changes between events, and deadlines can be a day away.

hints: Only three kinds of moments matter: a submission, a finish and a cancel. Jump from one to the next.
Keep each model's running requests in a min-heap of finish times, so the next free slot is the heap's top.
Keep each model's waiting jobs in a min-heap keyed by (deadline_ts, submit_ts, position). A job stays in the heap while it still has requests to start.
You do not need a separate event for a deadline: a job whose deadline has passed can be expired the next time it reaches the top of the heap, or at the end.
Models never interact, so you can simulate each model on its own.
followups: Show a small case where serving jobs in submission order expires more requests than earliest-deadline-first, and one where earliest-deadline-first is still not the order that expires the fewest requests.
Requests of a job can run in parallel up to a per-job cap as well as the per-model cap. What changes in your data structures?
The runner must decide in real time, without knowing future submissions. Which parts of your replay carry over, and how would you choose slot limits per model from a week of replays?
Owners want to know at submission time whether a job will finish before its deadline. How would you estimate that, and how wrong can the estimate be?

rules.ask: Deadlines are up to a day away and most seconds have no event. How many iterations does your loop do, and how do you jump between events?
Thousands of jobs are waiting. What does finding the earliest deadline cost at each of 200 000 starts, and what structure makes it O(log n)?
Two jobs wait: one submitted earlier with a deadline tomorrow, one later with a deadline in ten minutes. Which runs first under your rule, and what does the specification say?
Do you need an event at each deadline, or can expiry be decided lazily? What is the cost of each choice?

templates.title: Safety evaluation plan under an accelerator budget
templates.subtopic: tree knapsack, dependency closure, iterative traversal

sections.scenario: Before a model release candidate ships, a safety team runs evaluation suites against it. Each risk area has a base suite, and extensions of a suite (multi-turn, multilingual, tool-use, long-context and adversarial variants) reuse its harness, prompts and graders, so an extension can only run if the suite it extends runs too. Every suite has an estimated cost in accelerator-hours and a coverage score the team assigns. The compute for this run is fixed, and the team wants the planner that chooses which suites to run. {{depth_rule}}
sections.problem: Implement plan_evals(suites, budget, required). suites is a list of (suite_id, parent_id, hours, coverage), where parent_id is None for a base suite. A plan is a set of suites in which every suite's parent is also in the plan, with total hours at most budget. Return (coverage, hours), the totals of the plan with the greatest total coverage; among plans with equal coverage, the one with the fewest hours. The empty plan (0, 0) is always allowed when nothing is required. {{gate_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 3 000 suites; budget up to 2 000; hours from 0 to 60 and coverage from 0 to 100, all integers. Suites arrive in any order (an extension may be listed before its parent); every parent_id exists and there are no cycles. A family can be thousands of suites deep. O(n · budget) time is expected, with no recursion-depth failure.
sections.assumptions: Suites, hours and coverage scores are hypothetical. Coverage is treated as additive, which is a simplification the follow-ups question. A suite in the plan runs once.
sections.criteria: Recognises a precedence-constrained (tree) knapsack; enforces the parent rule; inclusive budget; correct tie-break on hours; required suites force their ancestors and give None when they cannot fit; handles children listed before parents, zero-hour suites and very deep families without recursion; O(n · budget) time; explains why greedy by ratio fails and what a DAG of prerequisites changes.

clarifications.q: Can an extension run without the suite it extends?
clarifications.a: No. Every suite in the plan needs its parent in the plan, and so on up to the base suite.

clarifications.q: Is the budget inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A plan using exactly budget hours is allowed.

clarifications.q: Two plans have the same coverage. Which one do I return?
clarifications.a: The one with fewer hours. You return totals only, so any further tie does not matter.

clarifications.q: Can a suite cost 0 hours?
clarifications.a: Yes, when it only regrades results that already exist. It is still subject to its parent rule.

clarifications.q: What do I return when the required suites cannot all fit?
clarifications.a: None. With an empty required, the answer is never None.

hints: Enumerating subsets is 2ⁿ. This is a knapsack in which taking a suite is what makes its children available.
List the suites in depth-first order. At each position, either run the suite and move to the next position (its first child), or skip it and jump past its whole subtree.
Or pass a budget array down the tree: a child starts from the array its parent produces once the parent is taken, and a suite's result is the element-wise better of skipping and taking.
Fold the tie rule into the comparison: compare (coverage, −hours), or use coverage × M − hours with M larger than any possible total of hours.
A suite that is required, or has a required suite below it, cannot be skipped.
followups: Return the chosen suites as well as the totals. What extra state do you keep, and how much memory does it cost?
A multilingual tool-use suite needs both the multilingual and the tool-use suites to run. The dependencies are now a DAG. What happens to your algorithm, and what would you do in practice?
Two suites that probe the same behaviour overlap, so their coverage is not additive. How would you model diminishing returns, and what does it do to the dynamic programme?
Hours are estimates, and some suites overrun. How would you schedule the chosen plan so that an overrun cannot push a required suite out of the budget?

rules.ask: Give a small forest where taking the best coverage per hour first loses. What does an expensive base suite do to the ratio of its extensions?
One family is 2 500 suites deep. What happens to a recursive solution in CPython, and how do you make it iterative?
How many plans are there with 3 000 suites, and what structure lets you avoid looking at them?
Merging each child's table into its parent's costs budget² per edge. What is the total at 3 000 suites and 2 000 hours, and how do you get to O(n · budget)?

templates.title: Debug the pairwise win-rate report for two model snapshots
templates.subtopic: retries, position-swap normalisation, ties, pairing, macro averages

sections.scenario: A model team compares a candidate model snapshot with the current baseline snapshot on a fixed prompt set, using a grader model as judge. To cancel out position bias, every item is judged twice: once with the baseline's response shown first (AB) and once with the candidate's response shown first (BA). The judge answers which position was better, or a tie. A report gives the candidate's win rate per category and a macro average across categories. Reviewers noticed that the candidate's numbers move when nothing changed, that ties seem to hurt it, and that a category with two items swings the summary more than it should. {{retry_rule}}
sections.problem:
Fix win_rates(judgments) so that it meets this specification. Each judgment is a dict {"item", "category", "order", "attempt", "verdict"}; order is "AB" (baseline shown first) or "BA" (candidate shown first); verdict is "first", "second", "tie" or "invalid" (the judge's answer could not be parsed). Judgments arrive in any order.

  1. For each (item, order), only the judgment with the highest attempt counts. If that judgment is "invalid", the order is missing; an earlier attempt does not replace it.
  2. An item is paired when both of its orders have a counted, valid verdict. Every other item that appears is unpaired and contributes nothing else.
  3. For each order of a paired item, the candidate earns 2 points for a win, 1 for a tie and 0 for a loss. In AB the candidate is the response shown second; in BA it is the one shown first. A paired item is worth 4 points at most.
  4. Return {"categories": {category: {"items", "points"}}, "unpaired", "macro_win_rate"}. Only categories with at least one paired item appear. macro_win_rate is the mean, over those categories, of points / (4 × items); it is None when no item is paired.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 judgments; one pass plus work per item. An item always has the same category.
sections.assumptions: Items, categories, attempts and verdicts are hypothetical. Judging every item in both orders is a common way to reduce position bias in pairwise model comparisons; the scoring rule above is this exercise's specification. attempt values for one (item, order) are distinct.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its symptom; keeps the highest attempt independent of arrival order and does not fall back from an invalid latest attempt; normalises the position swap; gives ties half the points; requires both orders for a pair and counts the rest as unpaired; macro average over categories with None for no data; minimal fix that keeps the output shape; a test per bug.

clarifications.q: The judge was retried after a timeout. Which answer counts?
clarifications.a: The highest attempt, regardless of the order in which judgments arrive.

clarifications.q: The latest attempt is invalid but an earlier one parsed. Can I use the earlier one?
clarifications.a: No. The latest attempt decides; that order is missing.

clarifications.q: What does "first" mean in a BA judgment?
clarifications.a: The response shown first, which in BA is the candidate's. The verdict names a position, not a model.

clarifications.q: Is the summary weighted by items?
clarifications.a: No. Each category counts once: it is the mean of the per-category rates.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. Each has a test named after it.

hints: Read the deduplication loop and ask which judgment survives when attempt 1 arrives before attempt 2.
Write out the four cases (AB/BA × first/second) and who wins each.
Count the points for an item judged "tie" in both orders by hand.
What makes an item paired? Count the orders the code requires.
Compute the summary for one category with 2 items and another with 6 items, both ways.
followups: Write the smallest set of unit tests that would have caught every one of these bugs.
The macro win rate moves by 0.03 between two runs on the same snapshots. How would you put a confidence interval on it, and what is the right unit of resampling?
The candidate wins far more often in BA than in AB. What does that tell you about the judge, and what would you report?
Grader prompts change between runs. How do you store judgments so that two reports are only compared when they used the same grader version and prompt set?

rules.ask: A retry is logged before the attempt it replaced. What does "last seen wins" keep, and what does the specification want?
Attempt 2 is invalid and attempt 1 parsed. What does your code count for that order, and what does rule 1 say?
One category has 2 items and another 600. What does pooling do to the summary, and why does the report want a macro average?
Points are integers and the rate is a ratio. Where would you round, if anywhere, and what would rounding early do to the macro average?

templates.title: Incremental document enrichment through the Message Batches API
templates.subtopic: change detection, asynchronous jobs, idempotent results, versioned backfills

sections.scenario: A company that manages contracts for its customers enriches every document in its store with a model: {{fields}} structured fields such as document type, parties, renewal date, governing law and a short summary. The corpus holds {{documents}} documents and about {{daily_change}} of them are added or changed each day. The enrichment does not need an immediate answer, so the team uses an asynchronous batch interface of the kind public model APIs document (for example a Message Batches API): requests are submitted in batches, each request carries a caller-chosen custom id, processing completes within a window, results are retrieved afterwards and matched to requests by that id, and each request ends as succeeded, errored, canceled or expired. Enriched fields must be available {{deadline}}.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from "a document changed" to "its enriched fields are in the lakehouse table, with lineage". Cover change detection, how requests and custom ids are built, batch sizing and submission under the organization's usage limits, polling and result retrieval, matching and validating results, retries of errored and expired requests, idempotent writes, the versioning of prompt, model snapshot and output schema, and how a prompt or model change is backfilled across the corpus without starving the daily run.
sections.constraints: A document's fields must come from one prompt version and one model snapshot, never a mix. Re-running any step must not duplicate rows or bill the same work twice by accident. Usage limits apply to the whole organization, which other teams share. Results can be retrieved only for a limited period after a batch ends. Document text may contain customer personal data and must not be copied into logs.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, rates and deadlines are hypothetical; batch-size limits, processing windows, result retention and batch pricing are as the provider's current documentation states, and the design should not depend on exact values. Documents have stable ids and a content hash can be computed.
sections.criteria: Change detection by content hash; a work unit keyed by document, content hash, prompt version and model snapshot; deterministic custom ids recorded before submission; results matched by id, validated against a schema, and written idempotently with a version guard; distinct handling for errored, expired, canceled and invalid outputs; daily run and backfill separated with their own budgets inside shared organization limits; lineage columns on every row; no document text in logs; reasons about cost and the retrieval window.

clarifications.q: Do results come back in the order requests were submitted?
clarifications.a: Do not assume so. Match every result by its custom id.

clarifications.q: What happens to requests that are not processed within the window?
clarifications.a: They come back as expired. Deciding what to do with them is part of your design.

clarifications.q: Can a document change again while its earlier version is still being processed?
clarifications.a: Yes. The newest version must win, whatever order results come back in.

clarifications.q: How do we know the output is well formed?
clarifications.a: Ask for structured output (for example a JSON object or a tool call with a schema) and validate it; a response that does not validate is a failure, not a value.

clarifications.q: Who else uses the organization's limits?
clarifications.a: Interactive products. They must not be throttled by your backfills.

hints: Make the unit of work (document id, content hash, prompt version, model snapshot). If that tuple already has a valid result, there is nothing to do.
Derive the custom id from that tuple (or from a key that maps to it), so a result identifies exactly which version it describes.
Separate the daily incremental run from backfills: different queues, priorities and budgets, the same idempotent writer.
A request that succeeded but whose output does not validate is as much a failure as an errored one, and it was still billed.
followups: Walk through a crash after a batch was submitted but before its id was recorded. How do you avoid submitting the same documents again?
A document changes while its previous version is in a running batch. Show the rows written when the two results come back in the wrong order.
The prompt changes. How do you backfill {{documents}} documents within the usage limits, and what does the table show while the backfill is half done?
Ten percent of results in one batch fail validation. How do you tell a prompt problem from a model problem from bad documents, and what do you retry?
Estimate the daily cost of the incremental run from the change rate, and say which design choices change it most.

rules.ask: Two edits land in the same second. Which version does your change detection see, and why is a content hash safer?
Which results do you resubmit: errored, expired, invalid output? For each, how do you make sure the retry cannot overwrite a newer version's result?
If the custom id is random, how does a result tell you which document version and prompt version it belongs to after a crash?
Why did the team choose asynchronous batches for this, and what would the synchronous path cost in limits and money?
What is your merge key, and what condition stops an older version's result from replacing a newer one?

incidents: A backfill for a new prompt version is submitted at full speed and interactive products in the same organization start receiving rate-limit errors.
A batch ends with 30% of its requests expired on a day when daily changes were at {{daily_change}} plus a large customer import.

templates.title: Chargeback of model usage to business units
templates.subtopic: incremental pulls with restatement, SCD ownership, cost allocation, reconciliation

sections.scenario: A global enterprise uses a model API across {{workspaces}} workspaces and {{api_keys}} API keys. Finance must charge the cost back every month to {{business_units}} business units, and teams want daily spend by product. Public admin documentation for such APIs describes usage and cost reports grouped by time bucket, workspace, API key and model, with input tokens split into uncached input, cache writes and cache reads, plus output tokens, and with batch and standard processing priced differently. Ownership of keys and workspaces lives in the company's own registry and changes as teams reorganise. In this company's experience, figures for recent hours can still change for up to {{revision_window}} after they first appear, and only the monthly invoice is final.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from the provider's usage and cost reports to monthly chargeback and daily spend dashboards. Cover the incremental pulls and how revisions are absorbed, the grain and keys of the fact table, how cost is computed or taken from the reports, ownership history and allocation of shared or unowned keys, closing a month and reconciling it with the invoice to the cent, and who may see what.
sections.constraints: The month's chargeback must sum exactly to the invoice. A business unit sees only its own detail. A reorganisation in the middle of a month must not move earlier days' cost to the new owner. The pipeline must be safe to re-run for any day. Report APIs are rate limited, so pulls must be incremental.
sections.assumptions: All counts, windows and prices are hypothetical. The report endpoints return data at an hourly or daily grain and can be queried by time range. The invoice arrives a few days after month end in one currency.
sections.criteria: Incremental pulls with an overlap window and idempotent replacement at the report's grain; a fact table at hour × workspace × key × model × token type × processing mode; ownership as effective-dated history joined at usage time; explicit rules for shared and unowned keys; cost tied to the provider's figures or a versioned price table with a reconciled difference; a two-step month close with an adjustment line that makes the total equal the invoice; largest-remainder or equivalent rounding; per business unit access control; late corrections after close handled as adjustments, not silent rewrites.

clarifications.q: Can an API key be shared by several teams?
clarifications.a: A few are. The registry can say how to split them, for example by request tags or a fixed share; some keys have no owner at all.

clarifications.q: Do we compute cost from tokens ourselves or take the provider's cost figures?
clarifications.a: Your choice, but the result must reconcile with the invoice. Say what you do with the difference.

clarifications.q: How late can a revision arrive?
clarifications.a: Up to {{revision_window}} in this exercise; occasionally a correction appears later and must still be handled.

clarifications.q: Who owns cost after a team is merged into another?
clarifications.a: Days before the merge stay with the old owner; days after go to the new one.

clarifications.q: Is batch usage separate?
clarifications.a: Yes, it is priced differently, and teams want to see how much they saved by using it.

hints: Pull with an overlap: on every run, re-read the last {{revision_window}} and replace those buckets, keyed by the report's own grain.
Keep ownership as effective-dated rows (SCD type 2) and join usage to the owner valid at the usage hour.
Close a month in two steps: a provisional close from your data, then a final close that books the invoice difference to an explicit adjustment line.
An "unallocated" business unit is a feature: it makes missing ownership visible instead of hiding it in someone's total.
followups: A revision for a closed month arrives after the chargeback was sent. What happens to the numbers each business unit already saw?
The sum of your computed costs differs from the invoice by 0.3%. How do you find out why, and where does the difference go?
A key is moved from one workspace to another in the middle of the month. Which dimension do you attribute by, and why?
Product teams ask for cost per end-customer of their own application. What would you need from them, and what should never flow into this pipeline?

rules.ask: The same hour is reported three times as it is revised. How does your table avoid counting it three times?
A team was merged into another on the 15th. Whose budget does your join charge for the 3rd?
Cache writes, cache reads, batch and standard all have different prices. Where does your price table come from, and what do you do when it disagrees with the invoice?
You allocate a shared key three ways. How do you make the three parts add up exactly to the original cent amount?

templates.title: Streamed responses — event schema and time-to-first-token facts
templates.subtopic: streaming event schema, grains, latency facts

sections.scenario: A model API can stream its responses. Instead of one JSON body, the client receives a sequence of server-sent events: as public documentation describes them, a message start, then for each content block (text, a tool call's JSON input, or extended thinking) a block start, many deltas and a block stop, then a message delta carrying the stop reason and the final usage counts, and a message stop. Keep-alive pings can be interleaved, and an error event can arrive in the middle of a stream (for example when the service is overloaded). In this scenario the platform serves about {{daily_streams}} streamed requests a day, averaging {{events_per_stream}} events each, and the serving fleet emits one telemetry record per event. Product and infrastructure teams want time to first token, output speed, stalls and stop reasons by model, workspace and hour.
sections.problem: Design the data model from raw stream telemetry to analytical facts. Define: the telemetry event's schema (envelope, keys, ordering, and what a delta record stores, given that it must not store text); what is kept at event grain, for how long ({{raw_retention}}) and for which share of streams ({{sample_rate}}); the per-stream summary fact and the per-content-block fact, with their grains and columns; precise definitions of time to first token, time to last token, output tokens per second and the longest gap between deltas; and how a stream that never finishes (client disconnect, mid-stream error, host failure) is represented.
sections.constraints: No response text, thinking text or tool input is stored anywhere in the analytical model: only types, sizes, counts and timings. Every stream has exactly one summary row, including streams that never send a message stop. Hourly time-to-first-token percentiles by model must be available within 15 minutes of the hour ending. Event-grain data at {{daily_streams}} × {{events_per_stream}} events a day cannot be kept in full.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, rates, retention and the 15-minute target are hypothetical. Event names follow the public documentation in general terms. Telemetry is emitted server-side, each record carries the stream id, a per-stream sequence number and a timestamp from the serving host; what happens on the client after the bytes leave is not observable.
sections.criteria: Clear grains (stream, content block, event) with event data sampled by stream and kept {{raw_retention}}; named, precise first-token variants with queueing time separate; one summary row per stream including incomplete ones, closed by a timeout or a terminal event; idempotent, order-tolerant assembly by stream id and sequence number; no content stored; percentile-friendly storage (histograms or mergeable sketches); a versioned event contract; each incident traced to the grain or definition that caused it.

clarifications.q: When does the clock for time to first token start?
clarifications.a: You define it. The time the request was accepted and the time the first byte of the response was sent are both recorded; say which you use and keep queueing time visible separately.

clarifications.q: Does a thinking block or a tool call's first delta count as the first token?
clarifications.a: Decide and name it. Product wants "first visible text"; infrastructure wants "first token of any kind". Both may be needed.

clarifications.q: Does the pipeline receive events in order?
clarifications.a: Mostly. They arrive through a log partitioned by stream id, but retries can duplicate and reorder records within a stream.

clarifications.q: What does the message delta carry?
clarifications.a: The stop reason (for example end of turn, max tokens reached, a stop sequence or a tool use) and cumulative usage counts.

clarifications.q: Can a stream resume after a disconnect?
clarifications.a: Not in this scenario. A disconnect ends it.

hints: Separate three grains: the stream (one row per request), the content block (one row per block per stream) and the event (one row per event, sampled and short-lived). Most questions need only the first two.
Compute the timing columns once, when the stream closes, from its full event sequence: first delta, first text delta, last delta, delta count, longest gap. Then the deltas themselves can be dropped.
Sample by stream id, all or nothing, never event by event, so a sampled stream can still be replayed end to end.
followups: Write the exact definitions of time to first token and output tokens per second, including a stream whose first block is thinking and a stream with zero output tokens.
A stream never sends message stop: the client disconnected or the host died. When is its summary row written, by whom, and what does it say?
Why can hourly p95 not be computed by averaging per-host p95 values, and what do you store so that hourly and daily percentiles are exact or have a known error?
A stall alert must fire when more than 0.5% of a model's streams have a gap above 5 seconds between deltas. Which grain does it read, and how soon after a stall can it fire?
A new content block type ships next quarter. Show how the event contract and the summary fact evolve without breaking existing dashboards.

rules.ask: At {{daily_streams}} streams a day and {{events_per_stream}} events each, what does that table cost to store and scan for {{raw_retention}}, and which question actually needs it?
Do you sample events or streams? Show what event-level sampling does to the longest gap and the first-token time of a sampled stream.
The message start event is sent before the model produces any content. Is time to message start a useful first-token metric, and what would it hide?
Your dashboard shows mean time to first token. What does the mean hide that p95 and p99 show, and how do you combine percentiles across hours?
Two events of one stream carry the same millisecond, and a retry delivers one of them twice. What orders them, and what removes the duplicate?

incidents: A serving release starts sending the message start event before the request leaves the queue. The dashboard, which measures time to first token to the first event of any type, shows a 40% improvement nobody shipped.

About 2% of a day's streams have no summary row because the summariser writes one only on message stop. Most of the missing streams ended in a mid-stream overload error, so the error rate on the dashboard is too low exactly when it matters.

Event records were sampled at {{sample_rate}} one by one instead of by stream. Sampled streams now show gaps between deltas many times longer than real, and the stall alert fires every afternoon at peak.

templates.title: Tool-use calls across stateless requests
templates.subtopic: tool-use telemetry, linking calls to results, agent runs

sections.scenario: Developers give the model tools by sending each tool's name, description and JSON input schema with a request. When the model decides to use tools, the response ends with a tool-use stop reason and contains one or more tool-use blocks, each with its own id, the tool's name and an input. The developer's code runs the tools and sends a new request whose user turn carries a tool-result block for each tool-use id it answers (with the result, or flagged as an error). The API is stateless: every request resends the conversation so far. In this scenario about {{tool_share}} of the platform's {{daily_requests}} daily requests carry tools, a response can contain up to {{max_parallel}} tool calls at once, and a workspace typically defines {{tools_per_workspace}} tools. The platform wants to show developers and product teams tool error rates, how many round trips an agentic task takes, how often a tool call is never answered, and how long the round trip through the developer's code takes.
sections.problem: Design the data model for tool-use telemetry. Define the entities (request, response, tool definition, tool call, tool result, and an "agent run" if you introduce one); how a tool result in one request is linked to the call that a previous response emitted, without a conversation id; how resent history is recognised so that nothing is counted twice; how tools are identified and versioned; and the facts that serve the four metrics above, with their grains and exact definitions.
sections.constraints: Tool descriptions, inputs and results are customer content: the analytical model keeps only names, schema fingerprints, sizes, error flags, validity and timings. Each tool call is counted once, although its block is resent in every later request of the conversation. Metrics are reported per workspace and per tool. A tool's name is unique only within one request's tool list.
sections.assumptions: Volumes and shares are hypothetical. Tool-use ids are unique strings generated per call. A request may carry an opaque end-user identifier in its metadata if the developer chooses to send one; many do not. In this scenario only tools that the developer runs (client tools) are in scope.
sections.criteria: Tool call as the central fact keyed by tool-use id; results linked by id, first-seen semantics, duplicates absorbed; resent history recognised by ids, not positions; tools identified by workspace, name and schema fingerprint; an honest, stated definition of agent run and of round-trip time; unanswered calls with a defined timeout; no customer content stored; each incident explained by the linking rule it broke.

clarifications.q: Is there a conversation or session id?
clarifications.a: No. The API is stateless; you see each request in full and nothing else.

clarifications.q: How do I know which call a tool result answers?
clarifications.a: Each tool-result block names the tool-use id it answers.

clarifications.q: Can a developer edit history before resending it?
clarifications.a: Yes. They can drop, summarise or rewrite earlier turns, so a request is not guaranteed to extend the previous one exactly.

clarifications.q: Is a tool's name stable?
clarifications.a: Within a workspace usually, but two workspaces can give different tools the same name, and a tool's schema can change under the same name.

clarifications.q: What counts as a tool error?
clarifications.a: A tool result the developer flags as an error. Separately, a tool-use input that does not match the declared schema is worth tracking.

hints: Make the tool call the central fact: one row per tool-use id, opened when the response that emitted it is logged and completed when a result naming that id is first seen.
Each request resends history. A tool-use id or tool-result block you have already recorded is history, not a new event; key on the ids, not on positions.
Identify a tool by (workspace, name, schema fingerprint), not by name alone, and keep its versions.
followups: Define an agent run precisely enough to count "tool calls per run" without a conversation id. What breaks your definition?
A response contains {{max_parallel}} parallel tool calls and the next request answers only some of them. How are the others represented, and when do you declare a call unanswered?
The same tool-result block appears in five later requests. Show how it is recorded once, and which time is the result time.
A workspace changes a tool's input schema under the same name. How do error-rate trends stay comparable?
Product asks for a "task success rate" for agentic runs. What would you need that the API traffic does not contain, and what can you honestly report instead?

rules.ask: The API has no conversation id. Where would yours come from, and what happens to it when a developer edits history?
The developer summarises earlier turns before resending. What does your prefix hash do then, and how do you still link the tool result?
Two workspaces both have a tool called search with different schemas. What does your per-tool error rate mean?
Tool inputs and results are customer content. What do you keep instead, and how do you still investigate a schema mismatch?
The gap between a response and the next request includes the developer's tool, their own processing and the network. What can you honestly call that number?

incidents: A widely used client library retries timed-out requests with identical bodies. Tool results are now seen twice within seconds, and for some workspaces "answered calls" exceeds "calls".
The unanswered-call rate for a group of workspaces jumps from 3% to 28% overnight after their agent framework starts summarising history and dropping old tool-use blocks; their tools did not change.

A developer runs {{max_parallel}} parallel calls and returns the results in a different order from the calls. A pipeline that paired calls and results by position recorded correct results against the wrong tools, and two tools' error rates swapped.

templates.title: Enterprise seats, directory changes and adoption reporting
templates.subtopic: SCD type 2, member identity, effective-dated seats, periodic snapshots

sections.scenario: An AI assistant is sold to organizations on seat-based enterprise plans. An organization's admins give members seats either by hand or through directory sync from the organization's identity provider, which runs {{directory_sync}} and supplies attributes such as department, manager, cost centre and employment status. Members use the assistant on web, desktop and mobile. In this scenario there are {{tenants}} enterprise organizations, the largest with {{largest_tenant_seats}} seats. Each organization's admins want seats purchased versus assigned versus active, weekly active members by department and surface, and adoption curves for new cohorts; the account team wants the same across all organizations; and billing trues up each quarter on the peak number of assigned seats. Members leave, are deprovisioned, and sometimes return; departments are reorganised; occasionally two organizations merge after an acquisition.
sections.problem: Design the data model behind these reports. Define: the organization and the member (and what identifies a member over time); directory attributes as history; seat assignments as effective-dated intervals; the activity fact and its grain; precise definitions of an active member, seat utilisation and the quarterly peak; the rule that attributes activity to a department; how late or wrong directory changes are absorbed; what happens to a deprovisioned member's personal attributes after {{attribute_purge_days}} days while billing history remains; and how a merger of two organizations is represented.
sections.constraints: No conversation content enters this model: activity is counts by member, day and surface. A quarter's billed peak never changes after the quarter closes. Department reports attribute activity to the department the member was in on the day of the activity. Personal attributes of a deprovisioned member (name, email, manager) are removed {{attribute_purge_days}} days after deprovisioning; seat and activity counts stay.
sections.assumptions: Tenant counts, seat counts, the purge period and the quarterly peak rule are hypothetical (real plans and contracts differ). Directory sync delivers the current attributes of each member, without an effective date unless the identity provider supplies one. Times are UTC; organizations report in their own time zone.
sections.criteria: Stable member surrogate key with identity-provider id and email as attributes, plus a rule for returning members; directory attributes as type-2 history with late changes absorbed and restatements listed; seat assignments as intervals and an immutable quarter-close artefact; activity at member × day × surface with no content; precise definitions of active, utilisation and peak; department attribution as of the activity date; purge of personal attributes that keeps counts; an explicit merge model; each incident handled with validation of incoming syncs, identity resolution and correct peak computation.

clarifications.q: Is a member identified by email?
clarifications.a: Emails can change (a name change) and can be reused (a returning contractor). The platform assigns its own member id; with directory sync the identity provider's user id is also available.

clarifications.q: What counts as active?
clarifications.a: You define it. Product suggests at least one message sent by the member that day, on any surface.

clarifications.q: Can a member use the assistant without an assigned seat?
clarifications.a: Not normally, but activity in the minutes after a seat is removed can still arrive, and trials grant temporary access.

clarifications.q: How is the quarterly peak measured?
clarifications.a: You define the sampling: per day, per hour or exact intervals. Say why; billing will read it for years.

clarifications.q: Can admins see what members wrote?
clarifications.a: Not in this model. It is usage analytics only.

hints: Separate four things: the member (a stable surrogate key), directory attributes (type-2 history), seat assignments (intervals with start and end) and activity (a fact at member × day × surface).
Join activity to the attribute row valid on the activity date. A late directory change then restates a known set of days, which you can list and report.
Billing reads an immutable artefact closed at quarter end (a periodic snapshot or a frozen interval table), never the live assignment table.
followups: Define weekly active members and seat utilisation precisely. What do you do with activity on a day the member held no seat?
A sync that arrives on Thursday says a member moved department on Monday. Which rows change, and which already-published weekly numbers move?
The quarterly true-up bills the peak of assigned seats. Which table answers it, how is it computed, and why can it not change after close?
A member is deprovisioned and, after {{attribute_purge_days}} days, their personal attributes must go while billing history stays. Show the rows before and after.
Two organizations merge after an acquisition, and some people had seats in both. Model the merge so history before it stays correct and reports after it show one organization without double counting.

rules.ask: A contractor leaves and returns six months later with the same email; another member's email changes after a name change. What is your member key, and what do the cohort reports show for each?
A member moved from Sales to Support last week. Which department does their activity from last month land in, and is that what the admin expects?
The sync delivers a change late, effective three days ago. How does your type-2 table absorb it without overlapping intervals, and which published numbers change?
Weekly active is a distinct count over days. How do you get monthly active members without re-scanning activity, and why can you not add up weeks?
Your seat snapshot is taken at midnight UTC. A member is assigned at 09:00 and removed at 17:00 the same day. Is that seat in your peak, and should it be?

incidents: One {{directory_sync}} sync cycle sends an empty department for 30% of a large organization's members. The type-2 history records them all moving to "no department" and back, and that week's active-by-department report shows one department collapsing to a third of its size.

An organization re-provisions 1,200 returning contractors with their old emails. The model creates new member ids, the adoption report counts them as new adopters, and billing counts their seats twice for the day on which old and new records overlapped.

After an acquisition, two organizations are merged mid-quarter. The quarter's peak seat count adds both organizations' peaks although they occurred on different days, and members with seats in both are counted twice.

templates.title: Model aliases, snapshots and version comparison on production traffic
templates.subtopic: versioned dimensions, alias history, confounded comparisons

sections.scenario: A company runs {{apps}} applications on a model API, about {{daily_requests}} requests a day. Models are published as dated snapshots; an alias names a model's latest snapshot and moves when a newer one is released; older snapshots are deprecated and later retired on announced dates. Some applications pin a snapshot and some call an alias. Across the company {{snapshots_in_use}} snapshots are in use at once. Teams want to compare versions on their own traffic: latency, cost per request, stop reasons, user feedback (about {{feedback_rate}} of responses get a rating) and offline evaluation scores on sampled traffic, and the platform team must know who still depends on a snapshot that is about to retire.
sections.problem: Design the data model for model-version comparison. Cover: the model snapshot dimension and its lifecycle dates; the alias history and where its validity times come from; the request fact (what the application asked for, what served it, which application, key and prompt template version); feedback and evaluation facts that arrive later; experiment assignments where a team randomises; and the queries that answer "is snapshot B better than snapshot A for this application" and "which applications, keys and templates still reach a snapshot retiring on a given date".
sections.constraints: Each request is attributed to the snapshot that served it, never only to the name it asked for. A comparison holds the application and prompt template version fixed, or says plainly that it does not. Feedback can arrive up to 7 days after the response. The retirement report must list every dependent application at least 60 days before the retirement date.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, counts and rates are hypothetical. In this scenario each response names the model that served it, and every request is logged with the application, API key and workspace that sent it. Prices are effective-dated per model and may differ between snapshots.
sections.criteria: Requested name and served snapshot logged separately; snapshot dimension with release, deprecation and retirement dates; alias history derived from observations with announcement time kept apart; prompt template version on every request; late-arriving feedback and evaluation facts keyed by request; stratified or randomised comparisons with honest statements of confounding and of feedback bias; a retirement report from served snapshots; each incident traced to the missing column or definition.

clarifications.q: Does the response say which snapshot served an alias request?
clarifications.a: In this scenario, yes. Log it on every request.

clarifications.q: When does an alias move?
clarifications.a: When a newer snapshot is released. Record the announcement, and also the time you first observed a response from the new snapshot.

clarifications.q: Is user feedback representative?
clarifications.a: No. About {{feedback_rate}} of responses get any rating, and unhappy users rate more often.

clarifications.q: Do applications run controlled experiments?
clarifications.a: Some randomise by end user with an assignment table; most simply switch.

clarifications.q: Do snapshots write answers of the same length?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily. A newer snapshot may write longer or shorter answers for the same prompt.

hints: Log requested_model and served_snapshot as two columns. The alias history can be derived from them; you never need to guess which snapshot an alias meant.
Version the prompt template and log its version on every request. A model switch and a template change on the same day are confounded unless you can separate them.
Compare within strata (application, template version, task type) and weight to a common mix, or use the randomised assignment when one exists.
followups: An application called an alias all month and the alias moved on the 12th. Write the logic for "latency by snapshot" and for "latency by what the application asked for", and say who needs each.
A snapshot's feedback is 3 points worse, but most of its traffic is a new, harder task type. How does your model expose the mix shift?
A snapshot retires in 90 days. Produce the list of applications, keys and templates still using it, including any that reach it through an alias.
Design the experiment tables so a 50/50 comparison stays valid when requests in one arm fail and retry more often.
With {{snapshots_in_use}} snapshots across {{apps}} applications, how does the comparison dashboard avoid inviting conclusions from tiny cells?

rules.ask: Is that the name the application asked for or the snapshot that served it? What happens to your comparison the day an alias moves?
Only {{feedback_rate}} of responses get a rating, and unhappy users rate more. How do you compare two snapshots fairly with it?
What is the unit of randomisation, and what happens to your comparison if one arm times out and retries more?
Where do your alias history's valid_from times come from: the announcement, or the first response you saw from the new snapshot? When do they differ?
The newer snapshot writes longer answers. Is a higher total latency a regression? Which latency would you compare?

incidents: The alias that most of the {{apps}} applications call moved to a new snapshot on a Tuesday. A dashboard keyed on the requested model name shows a step change in latency and cost for "the same model", and one application team files a regression against its own code.
The largest application shipped a new prompt template version on the same day it pinned a newer snapshot. Its feedback rate drops, and two teams each blame the other's change.
A retirement report built from pinned snapshot names misses four applications that reach the retiring snapshot through an older alias that has not moved since it was released.

templates.title: Weekly task-category counts with small cells merged into “other”
templates.subtopic: aggregation thresholds, suppression into other, deletion and retention

sections.scenario: An AI assistant platform publishes aggregate insight into what people use it for: weekly counts of conversations by task category. No person reads conversations for this: an automated classifier assigns each conversation a task category, and only that label, a pseudonymous user key, the organization and timestamps reach the analytics model below. So that no individual or organization can be singled out, a (week, category) cell is published only when it covers enough distinct users and organizations; smaller cells are merged into one other row per week, which must clear the same threshold. Users can delete conversations, and organizations can opt out of analysis.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns week_start, task_category, conversations, users, orgs, ordered by week_start, task_category. The rules:

  • {{window_rule}}
  • A conversation counts when its organization has not opted out (orgs.analytics_opt_out is false), it has no row in deletion_requests (whatever the request's time), and it has a category. {{facet_rule}} A conversation with no facet row is unclassified and is not counted anywhere, not even in other.
  • week_start is the date of the Monday (UTC) of the week containing the conversation's created_at.
  • For each (week, category): conversations is the number of counted conversations, users the number of distinct user_key, orgs the number of distinct org_id. {{threshold_rule}}
  • All the cells of a week that are not publishable are merged into one row with task_category = 'other'. Its conversations, users and orgs are counted over the union of those cells' conversations (distinct users and organizations, never sums of the cells' counts). The other row is returned only when it meets the same threshold. A week whose cells are all publishable has no other row. No real category is called other.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). PostgreSQL. The sample has {{conversations}} conversations; production has hundreds of millions a week, so be ready to say how you would compute this incrementally.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, categories, thresholds and volumes. Real aggregation thresholds are far larger; small ones keep the sample readable. A user_key is a pseudonymous key that belongs to one organization. Timestamps are UTC.
sections.criteria: Each conversation settled once (window, opt-out, deletion, category) before aggregation; one facet row per conversation (the latest, and at the hardest level only rows known at the report time); Monday weeks in UTC; inclusive thresholds on distinct users and organizations; other counted over the union of the suppressed conversations and itself threshold-checked; deterministic ordering; can discuss differencing, incremental recomputation after deletions, and retention versus reproducibility.

clarifications.q: Are the thresholds inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. A cell with exactly the minimum number of distinct users (and organizations) is published.

clarifications.q: A user appears in two unpublishable categories in the same week. How many users does other have from them?
clarifications.a: One. Count distinct keys over the merged conversations.

clarifications.q: A deletion was requested after the report time. Is the conversation counted?
clarifications.a: No. A deletion is honoured whenever the report is run.

clarifications.q: A conversation was created at exactly Monday 00:00:00 UTC. Which week?
clarifications.a: The week that starts at that moment.

clarifications.q: Which time decides the week: creation or classification?
