clarifications.a: Creation. Classification time only decides which facet row is the conversation's category.

hints: Settle every conversation first, in one CTE with one row per conversation: is it counted, what is its category, which week is it in. Then aggregate.
Decide publishability per cell, then build other from the conversations of the cells that failed, by joining back to them. Adding up the failed cells' user counts is wrong.
At Hard and above, DISTINCT ON (conversation_id) … ORDER BY conversation_id, classified_at DESC picks one facet row per conversation.
followups: Suppose you also published each week's total. Could a reader recover a suppressed cell? What does merging into other protect, and what would still leak?
Make it incremental: a deletion arrives for a conversation in a week already published. What do you store, what do you recompute, and what do you republish?
A category is suppressed one week and published the next at exactly the threshold. Is there a differencing risk across weeks or across overlapping reports, and would you add rounding or noise?
Retention says data older than the window must not be used, but last quarter's published report was computed from it. What do you keep, and what do you tell someone who asks to reproduce that report?

rules.ask: Your other row adds up the users of the suppressed cells. A user in two of them is counted twice. What does that do to the threshold check?
Your LEFT JOIN keeps conversations that have no facet row. Where do they end up, and should they be counted at all?
HAVING removes the small cells. Where do their conversations go, and how do you build other from them?
Which day does your week start on, and in which time zone? What would BigQuery's default WEEK part give you?
Do you pick the latest facet among all rows, or among the rows that existed at the report time? Which one lets you reproduce the report?

incidents: The deletion pipeline was paused for three days. When it resumed, 1,900 deletions landed for conversations in weeks that were already published, and two published cells now fall below {{min_users}} users. The published numbers are on a public page.

The classifier was re-run over the past month with a new version, moving many conversations between categories. Last month's published figures no longer match a recomputation, and a reader asks which set is right.

templates.title: Stream health as the client experiences it
templates.subtopic: event sequencing, stalls, client-perceived SLOs

sections.scenario: Most calls to a model API's Messages endpoint are streamed as server-sent events: message_start, then for each content block a content_block_start, a run of content_block_delta events carrying text or fragments of a tool call's JSON input, and a content_block_stop; then message_delta (with the stop reason and the final output token count) and message_stop. Periodic ping events keep the connection alive, and an error event (for example, overloaded) can arrive in the middle of a stream. About {{daily_streams}} streamed responses a day are served from {{regions}} regions. Latency dashboards measured at the inference servers look healthy, yet enterprise customers report responses that start quickly and then hang, and streams that end without a message_stop. Leadership wants to measure stream health the way the client experiences it.
sections.problem: Design the stream-health observability platform. Cover what is recorded per stream and per event and where (the API gateway that holds the client connection, the inference server, optionally a client SDK); how one stream's events become one record; which metrics define health (time to message_start, time to the first content delta, inter-event gaps, stalls longer than {{stall_threshold}}, how a stream ended and who closed it first); how they are computed per model, region and organisation with {{freshness}} freshness; and how on-call tells a server fault from a client or network one.
sections.constraints: The content of deltas (text, thinking, tool inputs) never leaves the serving path; telemetry may carry sizes, counts, timestamps and identifiers only. Telemetry must not add measurable latency to the stream. Per-event detail is kept 7 days for debugging; per-stream summaries 90 days. An organisation's view is visible only to that organisation's admins and to internal on-call.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, thresholds and retention periods are hypothetical. The event types are those of the public streaming format. Gateway hosts and inference hosts have independent clocks that can drift by tens of milliseconds, sometimes more. Every request has a request id returned to the client.
sections.criteria: Measures at the point that sees the client (gateway) and summarises per stream at the edge; precise definitions of first content, stall and end type with who closed first; per-stream records joined with server records by request id under bounded lateness, using one host's monotonic clock for durations; percentiles from mergeable sketches; per-event detail sampled and short-lived; content never in telemetry; organisation-scoped access; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Where does "client-perceived" start and end?
clarifications.a: At the gateway: when it received the request, when it flushed each event to the socket, and when the socket closed. We cannot see the customer's network.

clarifications.q: Do ping events count as progress?
clarifications.a: No. A stream that sends only pings for {{stall_threshold}} or longer is stalled.

clarifications.q: Do we need every event long-term?
clarifications.a: No. Per-event detail for 7 days; a per-stream summary for 90 days.

clarifications.q: Who can end a stream early?
clarifications.a: Either side: the client disconnects (a user pressed stop, a timeout fired), or the server sends an error event or drops the connection.

clarifications.q: Does tool use change anything?
clarifications.a: Tool input arrives as JSON fragments in deltas and the stream ends with stop reason tool_use; the tool result comes back in a new request, so a multi-step agent turn is several streams.

hints: Summarise each stream where all its events pass, the gateway's connection handler, instead of shipping every delta and reassembling it downstream.
Classify how every stream ended (message_stop, error event, server close, client close) and record which side closed first.
Gaps are a distribution inside each stream. Keep per-stream maximum gap and stall count, then compute percentiles across streams with mergeable sketches.
followups: Define a stalled stream precisely, and show how you compute the stall rate per model and region within {{freshness}}.
A stream ends without message_stop. How does your record tell apart a client that left, a network failure and a server failure?
Gateway and inference-server records for the same request arrive out of order and with clock skew. How do you join them, and which clock do you trust for which metric?
An enterprise admin asks for their organisation's stall rate per API key and per workspace. What do you show, and what stops one organisation seeing another's data?
Server-side time to first token is flat, but complaints doubled. What would your platform have shown, and which metric did the old dashboards miss?

rules.ask: At {{daily_streams}} streams a day with hundreds of deltas each, what does shipping every event cost, and what do you summarise at the edge instead?
A stream sends message_start in 300 ms and its first text delta 9 seconds later. What does your TTFT measure, and is that what the customer felt?
Why does an average inter-event gap hide stalls, and what would you compute instead?
How long do you wait before a stream's record is final, and what happens to an event that arrives after that?
Client timings come from customers' machines. How do you sample, trust and store them, and what does the platform do for customers who never send them?

incidents: A load-balancer change sets an idle timeout shorter than the server's ping interval. Streams with a long pause before their first delta are cut with no error event, and the inference servers' dashboards stay green because the servers finished their work.

During an overload in one of the {{regions}} regions, 4% of streams end with an overloaded error event after content has started; client retries resend the whole request and roughly double that region's load.
A gateway deploy flushes events through a 64 KB buffer instead of immediately. Server-side timings are unchanged, but time to first visible text rises by several seconds for short answers.
Clock drift of 2 seconds on a subset of gateway hosts produces negative gaps on some streams and false stalls longer than {{stall_threshold}} on others.

templates.title: Workspace spend limits and cost attribution
templates.subtopic: near-real-time enforcement, priced ledger

sections.scenario: An organisation using a model API groups its API keys into workspaces, typically one per product team or environment. Each request's usage reports ordinary input tokens, output tokens, cache-write input tokens and cache-read input tokens. Prices are per model and per token class: cache writes cost more than ordinary input, cache reads much less, and requests sent through the asynchronous batch interface are discounted. Prices for some of the {{models}} models change a few times a year. Admins can set a monthly spend limit per workspace; once a workspace reaches it, further requests from its keys are rejected until the limit is raised or the month ends. Admins also want cost per API key and per workspace per day that matches the invoice exactly. The platform serves {{daily_requests}} requests a day from {{regions}} regions, and a crossed limit must take effect within {{enforce_within}}.
sections.problem: Design (1) cost attribution from usage records to cost per API key, workspace, model and day, consistent with the invoice; (2) spend-limit enforcement on the request path within {{enforce_within}}; and (3) the admin reporting view with corrections. Cover the price catalogue and its versions, where cost is computed, how batch usage that completes hours after submission is counted, how far a workspace can overshoot, how {{regions}} regions share one limit, and what happens when the enforcement path is unavailable.
sections.constraints: The limit check adds under 2 ms at p99 and makes no synchronous cross-region call. Overshoot above a limit must be bounded and stated. Invoice amounts are exact in fixed-point currency units, never floating point. An API key belongs to one workspace at a time, but keys can be moved between workspaces or archived. Organisation-wide request and token-per-minute rate limits exist and are enforced by another system; you own spend only.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, prices and limits are hypothetical. The monthly invoice is produced from the same usage records. Each request has a unique request id, and usage is known in full only when the request finishes.
sections.criteria: Exact priced ledger keyed by request id, separate from a fast regional counter; versioned price catalogue with effective times, cost in fixed-point at a stated grain; key-to-workspace attribution as of request time; a stated overshoot bound with admission estimates or reservations and post-hoc reconciliation; regional budget allocation without synchronous cross-region calls; explicit fail-open or fail-closed policy; reports reconcile to the invoice by construction; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery, customer remediation and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is a request's cost known before it runs?
clarifications.a: No. Input tokens are known at admission; output, cache-write and cache-read tokens only when it finishes.

clarifications.q: When does a batch request count against the limit and the invoice?
clarifications.a: Assume when its result is produced, which can be up to 24 hours after the batch was created.

clarifications.q: Can an admin raise the limit mid-month?
clarifications.a: Yes, and requests should be accepted again within {{enforce_within}}.

clarifications.q: A key moves to another workspace mid-month. Where does its cost go?
clarifications.a: Usage stays with the workspace the key belonged to when the request was made.

clarifications.q: Is the month in UTC?
clarifications.a: Assume yes for this design.

hints: Separate the exact priced ledger (one record per request id, idempotent) from the fast approximate counter the request path reads.
Cost is tokens times the price in force when the request was made. Version the price catalogue by effective time and store the version on each record.
Output cost is unknown at admission. Decide whether you reserve an estimate or check after the fact, and compute the worst-case overshoot either way.
followups: Walk one request from admission to its line on the invoice. Where is the price looked up, and where could the request be counted twice?
A workspace at 99.8% of its limit sends 2,000 concurrent long requests. How far can it overshoot under your design, and how would you shrink that?
A price change takes effect at midnight UTC while one region's usage stream is 40 minutes behind. Which price do the delayed requests get?
The counter store in one region is unavailable. Do you fail open or closed, for which workspaces, and for how long?
An admin's daily cost per key in the console differs from the invoice by 0.3%. Design the system so the gap can be explained line by line.

rules.ask: After a regional failover the counter and the priced ledger disagree. Which one wins, and how is the counter corrected?
Reserving against the maximum output length blocks a workspace early when it sends many long-limit requests. When and how is the unused part released?
What numeric type holds cost at each stage, and where does rounding happen relative to the invoice?
How much can one workspace spend while the check fails open, and who absorbs that cost?
A usage record is delivered twice after a consumer restart. What key makes the priced record idempotent, and where is it enforced?

incidents: A price update for one of the {{models}} models was loaded with the cache-write and cache-read prices swapped, and has been live for 6 hours.

An enterprise workspace keeps spending for 25 minutes after crossing its limit, far beyond {{enforce_within}}, because the counter in one of the {{regions}} regions stopped receiving usage after a consumer-group rebalance.
A large batch created on the 30th completes on the 1st. The customer's finance team asks why its cost appears in the new month.
An admin moves 40 API keys between workspaces mid-month, and the daily cost per workspace report counts their usage in both workspaces for that day.

templates.title: Safety signal monitoring and the human review queue
templates.subtopic: streaming aggregation, review prioritisation, privacy

sections.scenario: A model provider runs {{classifiers}} automated safety classifiers over traffic to its apps and API, each scoring requests or responses for one category of its usage policy. About {{daily_requests}} requests a day are scored. Individual scores are noisy; what matters are patterns: an account whose traffic is persistently flagged in one category, a sudden rise in one category across many unrelated accounts (a new misuse technique spreading), or a classifier whose flag rate shifts after a model or classifier update. A trust and safety team can review about {{review_capacity}} cases a day, and enforcement (a warning, restricting an account) requires a human review with evidence. Flagged material is kept for {{flag_retention}}; unflagged content is not kept for this purpose.
sections.problem: Design the monitoring pipeline: collecting scores, aggregating them per account and category over time, detecting persistent patterns and cross-account spikes, a prioritised review queue that fits the team's capacity, the evidence a reviewer sees, feeding review decisions back into measures of classifier quality, and monitoring the classifiers themselves. Cover who can see what, retention, and failure handling.
sections.constraints: Scoring must not add noticeable latency to requests. Reviewers see the minimum content needed, only for queued cases, and every access is logged. Some enterprise organisations have agreements under which request content is not stored; for them only scores and metadata may be kept. Flagged material is deleted after {{flag_retention}}. No enforcement action is fully automatic.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, capacities, categories and retention are hypothetical. An account is an organisation, and within it an API key or an app user; actions can apply at either level. Thresholds per category are set by the safety team through reviewed configuration.
sections.criteria: Scoring asynchronous to the request path; versioned classifiers and thresholds recorded on every flag; per-account, per-category windowed aggregates normalised for volume, plus cross-account spike detection keyed on category and shared features; a capacity-aware queue ranked by severity and confidence with sampled review of unflagged traffic for recall; minimal, logged reviewer access and content rules enforced before storage; retention enforced and checked; classifier monitoring with label feedback; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Are classifier scores calibrated probabilities?
clarifications.a: No. Each classifier has its own scale; thresholds are set per category.

clarifications.q: Does one flagged request start a review?
clarifications.a: Not on its own, except in the most severe categories. Patterns do.

clarifications.q: Can a reviewer see a whole conversation?
clarifications.a: Only the flagged turns with minimal context, unless they escalate with a recorded reason.

clarifications.q: Who changes thresholds?
clarifications.a: The safety team, through a reviewed change. Your platform must record which classifier version and threshold produced each flag.

clarifications.q: How fast must a spreading pattern be seen?
clarifications.a: Within an hour for a cross-account spike; daily is fine for slow persistent patterns.

hints: Separate per-request scores (huge volume, short-lived) from per-account aggregates over windows (small, and what drives review).
Rank the queue by expected harm and confidence, not arrival time. Review capacity is the binding constraint.
Every review decision is a label. Use labels to estimate each classifier's precision at its threshold, and watch for drift after model or classifier changes.
followups: How do you find an account whose flag rate in one category is persistently high without flooding reviewers with large accounts that simply send more traffic?
A new misuse technique appears across 3,000 small accounts within an hour. What detects it, and what does the review queue look like?
A model version upgrade changes one classifier's flag rate by 40%. How do you tell a classifier shift from a real change in behaviour?
A reviewer asks to see an account's full history. What does your design allow, and how is it audited?
You only review what the pipeline flags. How do you estimate what it misses, and how much review capacity do you spend on that?

rules.ask: Large accounts cross a fixed count just by sending more traffic. How do you normalise, and what does normalising do to very small accounts?
The constraints limit what is kept. What exactly is stored for a request that was not flagged, and for how long?
Capacity is {{review_capacity}} cases a day and the queue grows faster. Which cases are never reviewed under arrival order?
Reviewers only see flagged cases. How do you estimate recall, and what sample of unflagged traffic would you review?
Enforcement needs a human review. What may happen automatically before review, and what must not?

incidents: A classifier update changes its score scale. Flags in its category rise 9× within an hour, and the queue, sized for {{review_capacity}} cases a day, fills with low-value cases.
Flagged excerpts from an enterprise organisation whose agreement forbids storing content are found in the evidence store, 3 days after they were written.
A coordinated pattern spreads across thousands of new accounts, each below the per-account threshold, for two days before anyone notices.
The scoring service falls behind during a traffic peak; 6 hours of scores arrive late and the per-account windows for that period were already closed and acted on.

templates.title: Prompt-cache effectiveness analytics
templates.subtopic: counterfactual cost, miss attribution, privacy-safe identifiers

sections.scenario: A model API lets callers mark cache breakpoints in a prompt; the prefix up to a breakpoint is cached for a short lifetime that is refreshed each time it is read. Each response's usage reports cache-write input tokens, cache-read input tokens and ordinary input tokens: writes are billed above the ordinary input price, reads well below it. About {{cached_share}} of the {{daily_requests}} requests a day, served from {{regions}} regions, set breakpoints. Many customers get fewer hits than they expect: a timestamp at the top of the system prompt, tool definitions serialised in a different order, a prefix below the minimum cacheable length, or requests spaced further apart than the cache lifetime. The product team wants a cache-effectiveness view per workspace and API key, with likely miss reasons, estimated savings and spend wasted on writes that were never read, within {{freshness}}.
sections.problem: Design the telemetry and analytics behind that view: what the serving layer records about cached prefixes for each request (without content); how hits and misses are attributed to reasons; how savings are computed against a no-cache counterfactual; how results are aggregated per organisation, workspace, key, model and hour and served to customers in a console; how the same data helps capacity planning for cache memory; and how all of it stays private.
sections.constraints: No prompt content, and nothing from which content could be recovered, leaves the serving path. Prefix identity may be represented only by a hash salted per organisation. Assume caches are never shared between organisations. Token counts shown must match billed usage exactly; savings estimates may be approximate if labelled. Customers see only their own organisation.
sections.assumptions: All figures and prices are hypothetical. Cache lifetime and minimum cacheable length are configuration of the serving system. On each request the serving layer knows which breakpoints were read, which were written, and why a lookup failed when it can tell.
sections.criteria: Per-request cache telemetry with cumulative per-block salted hashes and no content; billed token classes carried exactly and reconciled with billing; counterfactual savings and unread-write waste per key and hour; miss attribution through per-organisation prefix state with confidence and a short expired-prefix memory; late-data re-aggregation; organisation-scoped serving with opaque ids; salt rotation planned; capacity view of working-set size; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can the serving layer tell an expired entry from one never written?
clarifications.a: Only if it remembers recently expired prefix hashes. Assume it can keep a short list of them if your design needs it.

clarifications.q: Do customers care about hit rate or money?
clarifications.a: Money first; hit rate is how they debug.

clarifications.q: Can customers see prefix hashes?
clarifications.a: Only within their own organisation and only as an opaque id that cannot be compared across organisations.

clarifications.q: Is a write that is never read waste?
clarifications.a: Yes. A write costs more than ordinary input, so an unread write costs more than not caching at all.

clarifications.q: How detailed must the view be?
clarifications.a: Per workspace, API key, model and hour, plus a top list of prefix ids by wasted spend.

hints: The counterfactual cost of a request without caching is all of its input tokens at the ordinary price. Savings are counterfactual minus actual, and can be negative.
Miss reasons need state across requests: the last time this organisation used the same prefix hash, and where its prompt diverged from the last cached one.
Hash prefixes block by block (cumulatively) so you can tell where two prompts diverge without storing either.
followups: How do you attribute a miss to "prefix changed", "expired" or "below minimum length", and how confident is each label?
A customer's hit rate is 4% and they insist their prompts are identical. What does your console show them?
How would you estimate what a customer saves by moving a timestamp out of the system prompt, or by spacing requests differently?
The capacity team asks how much cache memory a longer lifetime option would need. Can you answer from this data, and what is missing?
Show that per-organisation salted hashes cannot reveal that two organisations use the same prompt, including to your own analysts.

rules.ask: How is the salt scoped and rotated, and what happens to week-over-week comparisons when it rotates?
A key has a 90% hit rate but loses money on caching. How is that possible, and which metric would show it?
Requests with the same prefix are served in several regions. Where does per-prefix state live, and what happens to miss attribution across regions?
Token totals in the console must match billing exactly. Which numbers may come from samples, and which may not?

incidents: A popular open-source agent framework release starts inserting the current time at the start of the system prompt. Within a day cache-read tokens fall 60% across thousands of workspaces and write spend rises.
A serving deploy shortens the memory of expired prefixes, so most misses are labelled "never written" and the console tells customers their prompts change when they actually expire.

For one day the console's cache-read token total for a large workspace is 2% below the invoice: usage from one of the {{regions}} regions arrived more than {{freshness}} late and was never re-aggregated.
Salt rotation changes every prefix id at once; customers' "top wasted prefixes" lists reset and support receives tickets asking what happened.

templates.title: Privacy-preserving insight into how an assistant is used
templates.subtopic: aggregation thresholds, model-assisted extraction, retention

sections.scenario: Product, safety and policy teams want to understand, in aggregate, what people use an AI assistant for: which tasks, in which of {{languages}} languages, and how that shifts after a model release, without anyone reading individual conversations. The proposed approach: inside a restricted environment, a model reads each sampled conversation and extracts short, non-identifying facets (task, language, a one-line topic summary); facets are embedded and clustered; a model describes each cluster; and only clusters containing at least {{min_accounts}} distinct accounts are ever reported. About {{weekly_conversations}} conversations a week are in scope under a policy that defines which conversations may be used; enterprise and API traffic are out of scope.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline end to end: scoping and sampling; the restricted extraction stage; privacy layers (extraction instructions that omit identifying details, the distinct-account threshold, a final privacy check on cluster descriptions); clustering into a browsable hierarchy; storage and retention of every intermediate; the outputs and who sees them; how privacy and accuracy are evaluated; and cost per weekly run.
sections.constraints: No person reads raw conversations in this pipeline. Facets and embeddings are deleted after {{retention_days}} days; only threshold-passing aggregates are kept longer. No cluster with fewer than {{min_accounts}} distinct accounts may be shown, including by subtracting one report from another. When a user deletes a conversation, it must leave every intermediate that still exists. Model calls have a fixed weekly budget.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, thresholds, budgets and retention periods are hypothetical. Accounts have stable pseudonymous ids inside the restricted environment.
sections.criteria: Scope and sampling stated with uncertainty; extraction confined to a restricted environment with identifying details excluded by instruction and verified by measurement; distinct-account threshold applied after every filter, with a fixed set of approved dimensions to stop differencing; a final privacy check on descriptions; idempotent, budgeted model stages; retention and deletion propagated to every intermediate with evidence; synthetic-data evaluation of privacy and accuracy; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the threshold on conversations or accounts?
clarifications.a: Distinct accounts. One account with 500 conversations is one account.

clarifications.q: Can analysts filter by language or date?
clarifications.a: Only along dimensions approved in advance, and the threshold applies after every filter.

clarifications.q: How do we know facets carry no personal details?
clarifications.a: That is part of your design; propose how you would measure it.

clarifications.q: How often does it run?
clarifications.a: Weekly; release comparisons are week over week.

clarifications.q: Who sees the output?
clarifications.a: Named internal teams through a dashboard; nothing below the threshold, and no drill-down to conversations.

hints: Treat every stage as a privacy layer that can fail, and measure each one separately.
Applying the threshold after every filter, and limiting which filters exist, is what stops differencing.
Validate the whole pipeline on synthetic conversations whose true distribution and planted identifying details you know.
followups: How do you sample so that small languages and rare tasks still have usable precision, and how is the uncertainty shown?
An analyst runs the report for two overlapping date ranges and subtracts. How does your design stop a sub-threshold cluster leaking?
How do you test that the facet extractor never outputs names, contact details or rare identifying facts, and what is the acceptance bar?
A user deletes a conversation the day after the weekly run. What changes, and what does not need to?
Leadership wants to compare usage before and after a model release. What makes that comparison fair, and what would make it misleading?

rules.ask: The threshold counts accounts per cluster. What about a filter applied after clustering, or two clusters that differ by a handful of accounts?
What do you add noise to, how is the budget spent across weekly releases, and what does it cost small clusters in usefulness?
Re-clustering each week changes cluster ids. How do you track a theme across weeks without keeping anything that identifies an account?
Which intermediates exist after {{retention_days}} days, and how would you prove the rest are gone?

incidents: A prompt change to the facet extractor raises the share of facets naming a company or person from 0.1% to 3%; the weekly report shipped with three cluster descriptions that name a small business.
A cluster with 12 distinct accounts, below the {{min_accounts}}-account threshold, appears in the dashboard because a new language filter was applied after the threshold check.
The weekly run's model spend doubles because a retry loop re-extracts conversations that already have facets.
An auditor asks for proof that facets older than {{retention_days}} days are gone, including a debugging copy an engineer made two months ago.

templates.title: A safety evaluation number behind a release was wrong
templates.subtopic: data correctness behind a decision, disclosure

cause: a join that silently dropped test cases with no grader output
a deduplication step that collapsed distinct test cases sharing a long common prefix
a filter that left multi-turn conversations out of the denominator

sections.scenario: Your team owns the pipeline that turns safety evaluation runs into result tables and the summary that a model release review reads. A new model version shipped {{days}} days ago, in part on a summary showing it at least as good as the previous version on a suite of harmful-request tests. An engineer on your team has just found {{cause}}. With the bug fixed, the new version scores {{delta}} worse than reported on that suite. The release review, safety researchers and product leadership all relied on the number. You lead the team.
sections.problem: How do you lead from here: the first hour, the first days and the following weeks? Cover confirming the finding, who you tell and in what words, how you correct the record, how you help the people who own the release decision decide whether anything changes (you do not own that decision), how you find what else the bug touched, and how you prevent a repeat. Then tell me about a real time a number your team produced turned out to be wrong after someone had acted on it (STAR, with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: You do not own the release decision. Published result tables are append-only; a correction is a new, linked version. Other suites may share the same code path. Your team has committed work for the next release.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical. The number appeared only in internal review material.
sections.criteria: Time-boxed reproduction and early, factual notice to decision owners; correction published as a linked new version with uncertainty; decision rights respected while giving owners what they need; blast radius found by lineage and recomputation prioritised by decisions affected; blameless review with invariants (row counts in = row counts scored, denominators checked) owned and tested; real example has measurable evidence and a personal contribution, or is honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the finding confirmed?
clarifications.a: One engineer's analysis. Nobody has reproduced it yet.

clarifications.q: Does a {{delta}} change matter?
clarifications.a: That is for the release owners to judge with corrected data and its uncertainty; your job is to give them that.

clarifications.q: Did other suites use the same step?
clarifications.a: Probably several. Nobody knows how many.

clarifications.q: Is the engineer who wrote the bug on your team?
clarifications.a: Yes, and they are upset about it.

hints: Reproduce before you broadcast, but time-box it to hours, not days, and tell decision owners early that a check is under way.
Say what you know, what you do not, and when you will know more.
Find the blast radius from lineage: every result that passed through the faulty step.
followups: Reproduction is taking longer than expected and a leader asks you for a yes or no today. What do you say?
The corrected score is inside the suite's confidence interval around the old one. How do you present that without minimising it or causing alarm?
The same step fed 11 other suites over six months. How do you decide which to recompute first?
Which check would have caught this before the review, who owns it now, and how do you know it works?
In your real example, what did you personally do, and what changed afterwards?

rules.ask: That decision belongs to the release owners. What do you put in front of them, and how do you avoid deciding for them through the way you frame it?
People made a decision on the old number. Who must hear about the correction, from whom, and how fast?
What did you personally do or decide?
Name the invariant that would have failed, for example test cases in equals test cases scored. Where does it run, and what happens when it fails?
How do you keep the review blameless while still being clear about what went wrong?

templates.title: Retiring a model version that customers still depend on
templates.subtopic: model deprecation, customer migration evidence

blocker: a regression on strict structured outputs for a few large customers
different tool-use behaviour that breaks some agent workflows
a higher cost per completed task for customers with long prompts

sections.scenario: A model version is due to be retired in {{weeks}} weeks under a published deprecation notice. {{tenants}} organisations still send {{share}} of API traffic to it. Customer-facing teams report that some of them will not move because of {{blocker}}. You lead the data team asked to supply the evidence for the migration programme: who is affected and how much, whether the blocker is real and how widespread, and progress every week. Product leadership owns the retirement date and will decide whether to hold it.
sections.problem: Plan and lead the work from the first week to the retirement date. Cover the analyses you would run and on what data, how you test the blocker without reading customer content, how you work with customer-facing teams, model teams and leadership, and what you recommend about the date and how you present it. Then tell me about a real migration or deprecation that affected customers or internal users where you led the evidence or the plan (with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: Customer content is not inspected; you have usage metadata (model, organisation, workspace, token counts, stop reasons, whether tools, caching or batch were used) and whatever customers choose to share. The date is public, so changing it has a cost. Your team has other commitments.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Fast segmentation of remaining traffic by organisation and feature use; blocker turned into a testable claim measured without customer content; tailored plans for the largest tenants and scalable ones for the tail; one agreed progress metric; a recommendation on the date that weighs evidence, cost of delay and fairness to customers who moved; clear decision rights; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do we know which organisations use which features?
clarifications.a: From usage metadata, yes: tool use, caching, batch, output lengths, stop reasons. Not from content.

clarifications.q: Can the blocker be tested?
clarifications.a: With public or synthetic evaluation sets, and with examples customers choose to share.

clarifications.q: Who decides on the date?
clarifications.a: Product leadership. You provide evidence and a recommendation.

clarifications.q: How concentrated is the remaining traffic?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet. That is your first analysis.

hints: Segment early: a few large organisations and a long tail need different plans.
Turn "will not move" into a measurable claim you can test.
Agree one weekly progress number with everyone, and define it so it cannot be gamed.
followups: Three organisations account for half the remaining traffic. What do you do differently for them?
Your tests reproduce the blocker for one of four reported patterns. What do you recommend, and to whom?
Two weeks before the date, a fifth of the original traffic remains. Hold or extend? Make the case either way.
In your real example, how did you measure progress, and what surprised you?

rules.ask: Customer content is not inspected. How else do you learn what breaks for them?
What does extending cost, and who pays it, including the customers who already migrated on time?
Which single number goes at the top, and what would make it misleading?
What did you personally decide or recommend?

templates.title: The latency dashboard is green; customers say streaming is slow
templates.subtopic: redefining an SLO, cross-team evidence

metric: median time to first token measured at the inference servers
p95 time to first token excluding requests that ended in an error

sections.scenario: For a quarter, the official latency metric, {{metric}}, has met its objective and been reported to leadership every week. Over the same quarter, {{complaints}} enterprise support tickets said streamed responses hang in the middle of an answer or take a long time before any text appears. {{teams}} teams own parts of the path (gateway, routing, inference serving, client SDKs), and your data team owns the metrics pipeline. Each team says its own numbers are fine. You suspect the official metric measures the wrong thing.
sections.problem: How would you lead this to a resolution? Cover how you establish the evidence, how you get the teams to agree what "slow" means for a streamed response, how you change an official metric that leadership has seen green for a quarter, and how you handle the fact that the new numbers will look worse. Then tell me about a real time you changed a metric people were attached to, or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: You own the metrics pipeline, not the services and not the objective itself. Customer content is not inspected; timings and event metadata only.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Evidence from traced tickets before argument; a metric definition grounded in what customers experience (first visible content, pauses, incomplete streams), per customer as well as per request; side-by-side period and a written translation from old to new; candid presentation of the historical miss without blame; agreement through the objective's owners; guardrails against gaming; real example with measurable outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do we have client-side timings?
clarifications.a: Not today. The gateway can record when each streamed event is sent to the client.

clarifications.q: Who owns the objective?
clarifications.a: An engineering leadership group. Teams propose changes to it.

clarifications.q: Are the tickets reproducible?
clarifications.a: A few include request ids; most do not.

hints: Start from the tickets that include request ids and trace them end to end.
Propose measures that match what a customer feels: time to first visible content, the longest pause between content events, streams that end without completing.
Run old and new side by side before switching, and publish how they relate.
followups: The new metric shows the objective was missed every week last quarter. How do you present that to leadership?
One team says the pauses are client network problems. What evidence settles it?
How do you stop the new metric being ignored or gamed the way the old one was?
In your real example, who resisted the change, and why?

rules.ask: A percentile of which population: requests, streams or customers? A customer with 5% of traffic can sit in the worst 1% all day.
How do you keep the investigation about the system rather than about a team?
Leadership has seen green for a quarter. How do you introduce a metric that is red on its first day?
Who disagreed, and what did you do about it?

templates.title: Tool-use telemetry that dozens of teams parse differently
templates.subtopic: schema evolution with many consumers, data contracts

trigger: a new kind of tool whose call metadata does not fit the existing fields
a privacy review finding that some log lines include tool arguments
a request to report tool-call success rates to enterprise admins

sections.scenario: Every turn in which the model calls a tool writes a telemetry line (tool name, number of calls, latency, outcome, stop reason) as a free-form JSON blob whose fields grew over time without a schema. {{consumers}} dashboards, jobs and notebooks parse it, each with its own assumptions, and changes to it broke consumers {{breakages}} times last quarter. Now {{trigger}} forces a change. You are the senior engineer on the team that owns the log.
sections.problem: How do you lead from here? Cover the decision between another patch and a typed, versioned schema under a data contract; how you find every consumer; how you migrate without breaking them; how you handle the immediate trigger; and how you get time and agreement from teams that do not report to you. Then tell me about a real piece of technical debt with many consumers that you reduced, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: The trigger has a deadline. Consumers belong to other teams with their own priorities. The log cannot stop during the migration.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Urgent risk handled first and separately; consumers inventoried from evidence; a typed, versioned schema with a contract checked in CI and an owner for changes; parallel run with a mapping, a dated end and usage-based proof that old fields are unread; a plan for orphaned consumers and holdouts; agreement won through cost of breakage in concrete terms; real example with measured reduction in breakage and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do you know every consumer?
clarifications.a: You know some. Access logs on the table and topic show more.

clarifications.q: How urgent is the trigger?
clarifications.a: Anything about what may be logged cannot wait for a migration; the rest has a quarter.

clarifications.q: Can two versions run side by side?
clarifications.a: Yes, at a storage and compute cost.

hints: Separate the urgent fix from the structural change, and do the urgent one first.
Find consumers from access logs, not from memory.
Run the old and new versions in parallel with a published end date and a field-by-field mapping.
followups: Ten consumers have no active owner. What do you do with them?
A consumer team refuses to migrate this quarter. What are your options?
How do you stop the new schema degrading into the old one in two years?
In your real example, how did you measure that breakage went down?

rules.ask: Who approves a change to the contract, and what happens in CI when a producer breaks it?
What happens to the consumers you did not find?
How long do both run, what does that cost, and what ends it?
How do you know nobody still reads the old field on the day you remove it?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a multi-tenant model API
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, scaling to multi-tenant workloads

angle: the data model and why it held up
the hardest correctness problem you solved
the biggest cost or performance decision
tenant_feature: cost attribution per workspace and API key
usage limits set per organisation and per workspace

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change at {{scale}} its load in a multi-tenant setting like an enterprise model API, where organisations group API keys into workspaces and expect {{tenant_feature}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at {{scale}} the load and with {{tenant_feature}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The multi-tenant setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with the alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible scaling analysis that names the first bottleneck; a concrete, incremental path to the tenant feature; own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a data system?
clarifications.a: It should move, store or compute data that others depend on; a service with a significant data model counts.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to schemas, keys, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the scaling question, name the first component to break and how you would know.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
At {{scale}} the load, which component fails first, and how do you know?
How would you add {{tenant_feature}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Why that over the obvious alternative, and what did it cost you?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
Where does tenant isolation live in your design: storage, the query layer or the application? What happens when one tenant is a hundred times larger than the median?
